distinguishing_feature: Right testicular pain is documented as localized to the right testicle; left testicular pain is localized to the left. Laterality is confirmed on exam, not by history alone.
Right testicular pain has a confirmed side; unspecified testicular pain is used when laterality has not been documented or the pain is bilateral/unclear.
Left testicular pain has a confirmed side; unspecified testicular pain is used when laterality has not been documented or the pain is bilateral/unclear.

Drug-induced erectile dysfunction has a clear temporal link to starting or changing a medication (e.g., antihypertensives, SSRIs); other male erectile dysfunction has an identified non-drug cause (e.g., vascular, neurogenic, hormonal) that isn't medication.
Drug-induced erectile dysfunction has a documented causative medication; unspecified erectile dysfunction is used when no cause, drug-related or otherwise, has been established.
Other male erectile dysfunction has an identified specific cause that isn't captured by a more specific code; unspecified erectile dysfunction is used when no cause has been identified or documented.

Corporo-venous occlusive erectile dysfunction is a specific vascular diagnosis (venous leak preventing erection maintenance), typically confirmed by penile duplex ultrasound; other male erectile dysfunction covers causes without this specific vascular confirmation.
Corporo-venous occlusive erectile dysfunction has objective vascular testing confirming a venous leak; unspecified erectile dysfunction has no such confirmed cause.

Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy follows removal of the prostate and surrounding tissue for cancer (higher nerve-injury risk); following simple prostatectomy follows removal of prostate tissue for benign disease (e.g., BPH), with lower nerve-injury risk.

Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy follows prostate removal; following radical cystectomy follows bladder removal, which also risks the neurovascular bundles but via a different surgical field and indication (bladder cancer, not prostate cancer).

Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy is linked to pelvic nerve-sparing surgery for prostate cancer; following urethral surgery is linked to procedures on the urethra itself (e.g., stricture repair), a different anatomical mechanism of injury.
Erectile dysfunction following radical cystectomy follows bladder removal surgery; following urethral surgery follows a procedure confined to the urethra, without bladder removal.
Erectile dysfunction following simple prostatectomy follows benign prostate tissue removal; following urethral surgery follows a urethral procedure, a distinct surgical site.
